To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

, in the early twentieth century, Taylor and his disciples sought to increase the power of the consumer to protect their interests by: (1) developing a science of consumer choice, (2) assisting consumers to gain access the information they required to make informed choices, and (3) providing consumers with a voice in the governance of the economy.

the scientific management movement, in the 1920s and 1930s, sought to empower consumers by (1) developing and promoting the concept of the consumer interest, (2) creating a new field of management knowledge, consumer research, and (3) establishing a number of organizations to assist consumers to access the information they required to protect themselves against the interests and practices of business.

Taylor and a small group of his colleagues sought to assist consumers to make informed decisions by: 1. developing and promoting the use of scientific management techniques to reduce the cost of consumer goods; 2. developing and promoting a science of consumer behavior; and 3. assisting consumers to gain access, through the media, to the scientific knowledge they needed to protect themselves from the vested interests of business.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which Taylor, and his colleagues, sought to create an environment in which the consumer could be empowered to make informed choices.
the following questions.
the history of the development of the consumer interest, and in particular, the ways in which the consumer interest was shaped by the ideas and actions of Taylor and his colleagues.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the scientific management of the American consumer was an important, but ultimately doomed, effort to establish an alternative to the market as the arbiter of social justice.
the consumer movement was the most important and most effective of all of Taylor's initiatives.
the scientific management of the American economy was not a monolithic, authoritarian body of thought and action.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Taylor's efforts were a major factor in the development of the consumer movement in the United States.
Taylor's efforts to create a scientific management of consumer interests were an important, if ultimately unsuccessful, contribution to the struggle for consumer rights.
, while Taylor was a strong advocate of the consumer, he was not a socialist.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the 1931s and 1940s, the Taylor Society, a body of scholars and professionals that had previously been regarded as a bastion of managerialism, became a leading advocate for the consumer.
the consumer movement of the 1970s was not as radical as many of its proponents claimed, and that the scientific management movement of the 1930–40s was not as conservative as its critics claimed.
the history of management is a history of contestation and that this contestation is not limited to the business world but extends to the wider society.
